domain:
    # N: number of samples (rows in original C array data[N][M])
    # M: number of features (columns in original C array data[N][M])
    s: dim in [0, N)          # sample index (row i in C code)
    p: dim in [0, M)          # feature / column index (j or i in C code)
    q: dim in [0, M)          # second feature / column index (j in C code)

data:
    # Input data matrix, matching C layout: data[i][j] is row-major,
    # and we model it as X[s, p] with row-major layout.
    X[s, p]: in num_t = (s, p) -> s * M + p     # row-major: samples × features

    # Output covariance matrix: cov[M][M] in C, also row-major.
    Cov[p, q]: out num_t = (p, q) -> p * M + q  # row-major: features × features

    # Temporary to store per-column means, mean[M] in the C code.
    mean[p]: temp num_t = p

parameters:
    float_n: num_t              # equals (num_t) N in the original code
    # The tile sizes and vector width are compile-time tunables.
    T_P: int                    # tile size for feature dimension p (e.g., 32)
    T_Q: int                    # tile size for feature dimension q (e.g., 32)
    T_S: int                    # tile size for sample dimension s (e.g., 64)
    V_Q: int                    # vector width along q (e.g., 8 for float32, 4 for float64)

computation:
    # 1) Compute per-feature means:
    #    mean[p] = (1 / float_n) * sum_{s=0..N-1} X[s, p]
    #
    #    This matches:
    #      mean[j] = 0;
    #      for (i = 0; i < N; i++) mean[j] += data[i][j];
    #      mean[j] /= float_n;
    mean_compute:
        for p:
            mean[p] = (1 / float_n) * sum(s, X[s, p])

    # 2) Compute covariance matrix:
    #    Cov[p, q] = (1 / (float_n - 1)) *
    #                  sum_{s=0..N-1} (X[s, p] - mean[p]) * (X[s, q] - mean[q])
    #
    #    This matches:
    #      cov[i][j] = 0;
    #      for (k = 0; k < N; k++)
    #          cov[i][j] += data[k][i] * data[k][j];  // after centering
    #      cov[i][j] /= (float_n - 1.0);
    #
    #    We express centering inline rather than storing a separate centered array
    #    to avoid an extra N×M buffer.
    cov_compute:
        for p, q:
            Cov[p, q] = (1 / (float_n - 1)) *
                        sum(s, (X[s, p] - mean[p]) * (X[s, q] - mean[q]))

dependencies:
    # Covariance must be computed after the means are available.
    for p in [0, M), q in [0, M):
        mean_compute(p) -> cov_compute(p, q)

optimization:
    # -----------------------------
    # Mean computation optimizations
    # -----------------------------
    # The cost of the mean phase is O(N·M) — smaller than the covariance phase
    # but still worth basic optimization.

    # 1) Interchange loops so that we iterate over samples s in the outer loop
    #    and features p in the inner loop, improving spatial locality on X:
    #    for s:
    #      for p:
    #        mean[p] += X[s, p]
    #    Since X is row-major in p, this makes accesses to X[s, p] contiguous.
    interchange(p, s)  # for the mean_compute reduction

    # 2) Parallelize across p after interchange: each feature’s mean is independent.
    #    This gives up to M-way parallelism, limited by the number of cores.
    parallelize(p)     # for the mean_compute reduction

    # 3) (Arithmetic) Precompute reciprocal of float_n once, then multiply by it
    #    instead of dividing inside mean_compute.
    #    # precompute_reciprocal(float_n) is a conceptual transform:
    #    #   r_float_n = 1 / float_n
    #    #   mean[p] = r_float_n * sum_s X[s,p]
    #    # This saves a division per p and preserves the mathematical result.
    # precompute_reciprocal(float_n)

    # -----------------------------
    # Covariance computation optimizations
    # -----------------------------
    # The covariance phase dominates runtime: O(N·M²). We treat it as a
    # matrix multiply of the centered data:
    #   Cov = (1 / (float_n - 1)) * (X_centered^T · X_centered)
    # where X_centered[s,p] = X[s,p] - mean[p].
    #
    # We apply standard GEMM-like optimizations: blocking, parallelism,
    # hoisting of invariant work, and vectorization.

    # 1) Block all three dimensions:
    #    - block(p, P, T_P): P indexes feature-tiles for p
    #    - block(q, Q, T_Q): Q indexes feature-tiles for q
    #    - block(s, S, T_S): S indexes sample-tiles for s (reduction dim)
    #
    #    This creates cache-friendly tiles of Cov and reuses sub-blocks
    #    of X across many multiply-accumulate operations.
    block(p, P, T_P)
    block(q, Q, T_Q)
    block(s, S, T_S)

    # 2) Parallelize outer tiles of (p, q).
    #    Each (P, Q) tile corresponds to a T_P×T_Q block of Cov that is
    #    independent of other tiles, given that the reduction over s is purely
    #    additive (no cross-tile dependencies).
    #
    #    We parallelize across the P dimension (feature tiles in p); for large M
    #    this delivers many independent tiles. T_P should be tuned so that
    #    (#P tiles) × (#Q tiles) ≥ number of hardware threads.
    parallelize(P)

    # (Optional, if a more aggressive runtime supports nested parallelism,
    #  we could also consider parallelize(Q), but this is typically less robust
    #  than parallelizing in a single outer dimension.)

    # 3) Choose an inner-loop order that exploits row-major layouts:
    #    Inside each tile (P, Q, S), use the loop order:
    #        for S (sample tiles)
    #          for s in S
    #            for p in P
    #              xp = X[s, p] - mean[p]          # hoisted across q
    #              for q in Q (vectorized)
    #                xq = X[s, q] - mean[q]        # contiguous along q
    #                Cov[p, q] += xp * xq
    #
    #    This is encoded via:
    interchange(S, P)   # hoist S (sample tiles) outside feature tiles
    interchange(S, Q)   # then iterate S outermost among P, Q, S inside cov_compute

    # 4) Hoist the computation of (X[s, p] - mean[p]) out of the inner loop over q
    #    within each tile, to avoid recomputing it for every q.
    #    Conceptually:
    #      hoist(p) inside cov_compute w.r.t. q.
    hoist(p)  # for centered value X[s,p] - mean[p] inside cov_compute

    # 5) Vectorize over q inside each (P, Q, S) tile.
    #    Since X is row-major in p (our "column" index), iterating q contiguously
    #    gives unit-stride accesses to X[s, q] and Cov[p, q], which is ideal
    #    for SIMD.
    vectorize(q, V_Q)

    # 6) Unroll a small factor of the reduction over s to reduce loop overhead
    #    and expose more ILP to the compiler. T_S should be chosen so that
    #    unrolling by 4–8 does not cause register spilling.
    unroll(s, 4)

    # 7) (Arithmetic) Precompute reciprocal of (float_n - 1) once and
    #    multiply at the end rather than dividing per Cov[p, q]:
    #      r_fnm1 = 1 / (float_n - 1)
    #      Cov[p, q] = r_fnm1 * sum_s (X[s,p]-mean[p])*(X[s,q]-mean[q])
    #    # precompute_reciprocal(float_n - 1) is a conceptual transform:
    # precompute_reciprocal(float_n - 1)

    # 8) (Optional, mathematical optimization) If bitwise-identical floating-point
    #    results are not required, we can exploit symmetry:
    #       Cov[p, q] == Cov[q, p].
    #    A symmetric schedule would:
    #      - Restrict cov_compute to p <= q (upper triangle),
    #      - After accumulation and scaling, mirror:
    #          for p, q with q < p: Cov[p, q] = Cov[q, p]
    #    This halves the arithmetic for the main reduction, at the cost of
    #    slightly different rounding behavior due to a different order of
    #    operations.
    #    This is left as an optional optimization and is not encoded above
    #    to preserve the original reduction pattern more closely.

```text
domain:
    # N = number of samples (rows), M = number of features (columns)
    i: dim in [0, N)          # sample index
    j: dim in [0, M)          # feature index
    p: dim in [0, M)          # covariance row index (feature)
    q: dim in [0, M)          # covariance column index (feature)

data:
    # C code: DATA_TYPE data[N][M]; accessed as data[i][j]
    # Row-major: consecutive j for fixed i.
    data[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Column means, length M.
    mean[j]: local num_t

    # C code: DATA_TYPE cov[M][M]; accessed as cov[p][q]
    # Row-major: consecutive q for fixed p.
    cov[p, q]: out num_t = (p, q) -> p * M + q

parameters:
    float_n: num_t                     # = (num_t) N
    inv_float_n: num_t                 # = 1 / float_n
    inv_float_n_minus1: num_t          # = 1 / (float_n - 1)

computation:
    # Precompute reciprocals once; avoids redundant divisions inside loops.
    inv_float_n = 1.0 / float_n
    inv_float_n_minus1 = 1.0 / (float_n - 1.0)

    # 1) Column means:
    #    mean[j] = (1 / float_n) * sum_{i=0}^{N-1} data[i,j]
    for j:
        mean[j] = inv_float_n * sum(i in [0, N), data[i, j])

    # 2) Center the data in-place (matches PolyBench C semantics):
    #    data[i,j] -= mean[j]
    #    After this, each column has zero mean across samples.
    for i, j:
        data[i, j] = data[i, j] - mean[j]

    # 3) Covariance matrix:
    #    cov[p,q] = (1 / (float_n - 1)) * sum_{i=0}^{N-1} data[i,p] * data[i,q]
    #    We exploit symmetry: cov[p,q] == cov[q,p], so only p <= q is reduced;
    #    the lower triangle is filled by mirroring.
    for p:
        for q in [p, M):
            cov[p, q] = inv_float_n_minus1 *
                        sum(i in [0, N), data[i, p] * data[i, q])
            cov[q, p] = cov[p, q]

optimization:
    # -------------------------------
    # Mean computation (stage 1)
    # -------------------------------
    # Each column mean[j] is an independent reduction over samples i.
    # Parallelize across columns; N is typically large enough that
    # each thread has substantial work per column.
    parallelize(j)

    # Small unrolling on the inner reduction improves ILP without
    # changing memory traffic; the factor is tunable.
    unroll(i, 4)

    # -------------------------------
    # Centering (stage 2)
    # -------------------------------
    # The 2D loop over (i,j) writes back into data[i,j].
    # We tile in both dimensions to improve cache locality and
    # vectorize across the feature dimension j, which is contiguous.
    block(i, I_c, 64)         # tiles of 64 samples (rows)
    block(j, J_c, 64)         # tiles of 64 features (cols)

    # Outer-loop over row tiles, then column tiles.
    hoist(I_c)
    hoist(J_c)

    # Distribute row tiles across cores; each (I_c, J_c) tile is independent.
    parallelize(I_c)

    # Within a tile, operate on multiple features at once via SIMD.
    vectorize(j, 16)          # 16-wide vectorization along contiguous j

    # -------------------------------
    # Covariance (stage 3)
    # -------------------------------
    # Treat covariance as a tiled symmetric rank-k update:
    #   C = data^T * data / (float_n - 1)
    # where data is N×M after centering.
    #
    # We block both feature dimensions (p,q) and the sample dimension (i)
    # to keep a P×Q tile of cov in cache while streaming through blocks of samples.

    # Tile the feature dimensions into 32×32 submatrices of cov.
    block(p, P, 32)           # tile index P over rows of cov
    block(q, Q, 32)           # tile index Q over cols of cov

    # Tile the reduction dimension i into chunks of 128 samples.
    block(i, K, 128)          # tile index K over samples

    # Loop order: P, Q, K, then inner p, q, i.
    # We first select a cov tile (P,Q), then accumulate partial sums
    # over successive K-tiles of samples.
    hoist(P)
    hoist(Q)
    hoist(K)

    # Parallelize independent covariance tiles across cores. Because we
    # only compute for p <= q (and mirror), each (P,Q) with Q >= P owns a
    # disjoint region of cov; tiles can be processed in parallel.
    parallelize(P)
    parallelize(Q)

    # Within a tile:
    #   - Make q the innermost loop to get unit-stride accesses in cov[p,q]
    #     and in data[i,q] (features are contiguous in memory).
    #   - i is the inner reduction loop; we keep it just outside q to
    #     reuse data[i,p] across multiple q.
    interchange(i, p)         # ... P, Q, K, i, p, q ...
    interchange(p, q)         # ... P, Q, K, i, q, p ...

    # Vectorize across q for efficient SIMD on the feature dimension.
    vectorize(q, 16)

    # Unroll a small number of i-iterations inside each K-tile to improve ILP.
    unroll(i, 4)
```

domain:
    # N: number of samples (rows), M: number of variables / features (columns)
    s: dim in [0, N)       # sample index, corresponds to C loop variable i
    f: dim in [0, M)       # feature index, corresponds to C loop variable j

    p: dim in [0, M)       # first feature index for covariance (C: i in cov[i][j])
    q: dim in [0, M)       # second feature index for covariance (C: j in cov[i][j])
    k: dim in [0, N)       # reduction index over samples (C: k in inner cov loop)

data:
    # Input data matrix: DATA_TYPE data[N][M]; row-major layout.
    # C access data[i][j]  ==  data[s=i, f=j] here.
    data[s, f]: in num_t = (s, f) -> s * M + f

    # Column means: DATA_TYPE mean[M]; contiguous 1D.
    mean[f]: tmp num_t = (f) -> f

    # Output covariance matrix: DATA_TYPE cov[M][M]; row-major.
    # C access cov[i][j] == cov[p=i, q=j] here.
    cov[p, q]: out num_t = (p, q) -> p * M + q

parameters:
    float_n: num_t                    # number of samples, equals (num_t)N

    # Tuning parameters (compile-time / launch-time constants).
    # Choose values appropriate for the target cache & SIMD width.
    T_p: int                          # tile size in feature dims p,q (e.g., 32)
    T_k: int                          # tile size in sample dim k (e.g., 128)
    V_mean: int                       # SIMD width for mean reduction over k (e.g., 8)
    V_cov: int                        # SIMD width for covariance reduction over k (e.g., 8)

computation:
    # ---------------------------------
    # 1. Column means (matches C code)
    # ---------------------------------
    #
    # C code:
    #   for (j = 0; j < M; j++) {
    #     mean[j] = 0;
    #     for (i = 0; i < N; i++)
    #       mean[j] += data[i][j];
    #     mean[j] /= float_n;
    #   }
    #
    # Here:
    #   mean[f] = (1/float_n) * sum_s data[s,f]
    #
    MEAN:
        for f in [0, M):
            mean[f] = (1.0 / float_n) * sum(k in [0, N), data[k, f])

    # -------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Covariance matrix (upper triangle + symmetry)
    # -------------------------------------------------
    #
    # C code:
    #   for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
    #     for (j = i; j < M; j++) {
    #       cov[i][j] = 0;
    #       for (k = 0; k < N; k++)
    #         cov[i][j] += data[k][i] * data[k][j];
    #       cov[i][j] /= (float_n - 1.0);
    #       cov[j][i] = cov[i][j];
    #     }
    #
    # after centering data[i][j] -= mean[j].
    #
    # We compute the same result as:
    #   X[s,f] = data[s,f] - mean[f]
    #   cov[p,q] = (1/(float_n-1)) * sum_k X[k,p] * X[k,q]
    #
    # Implemented directly without materializing X:
    #
    COV:
        for p in [0, M):
            for q in [p, M):    # restrict to upper triangle, as in original C
                cov[p, q] = (1.0 / (float_n - 1.0)) *
                             sum(k in [0, N),
                                 (data[k, p] - mean[p]) *
                                 (data[k, q] - mean[q]))
                cov[q, p] = cov[p, q]   # enforce symmetry: cov[j][i] = cov[i][j]

dependencies:
    # The covariance computation depends on finished column means.
    for f in [0, M), p in [0, M), q in [0, M):
        MEAN(f) -> COV(p, q)

optimization:
    # =================================
    # Mean-computation optimizations
    # =================================
    #
    # mean[f] is independent across f, so outer loop over f can be
    # safely parallelized. Inside each column, the reduction over
    # samples k is dense in memory if we traverse k in the natural
    # row-major order (s ≡ k).
    #
    MEAN:
        parallelize(f)              # distribute columns across cores
        vectorize(k, V_mean)       # SIMD across samples in the inner sum

    # =================================
    # Covariance-computation optimizations
    # =================================
    #
    # Mathematically, covariance is a centered Gram matrix:
    #     cov = (1/(N-1)) * Xᵀ X
    # with X[s,f] = data[s,f] - mean[f].
    # We schedule it like a blocked matrix multiplication to improve cache
    # locality and expose parallelism.
    #
    COV:
        # ---- Blocking / tiling ----
        #
        # Tile the feature indices p and q into T_p × T_p blocks so
        # that each thread works on a submatrix of cov that fits in
        # L2/L3 cache and can be reused while streaming through a
        # subset of rows.
        block(p, P, T_p)           # p = P * T_p + p_inner
        block(q, Q, T_p)           # q = Q * T_p + q_inner

        # Tile the reduction over samples k so that we read the input
        # data in cache-friendly stripes of T_k rows at a time.
        block(k, K, T_k)           # k = K * T_k + k_inner

        # ---- Parallelism ----
        #
        # Each (P,Q) tile produces an independent T_p×T_p block of the
        # upper triangle of cov (before mirroring), so we parallelize
        # across P (i.e., across feature tiles). Q remains serial to
        # avoid nested parallelism.
        parallelize(P)

        # ---- Vectorization and ILP ----
        #
        # Within each sample tile (fixed K) and feature tile (P,Q),
        # vectorize the inner reduction over k. This computes multiple
        # sample contributions to the same (p,q) pair in SIMD.
        vectorize(k, V_cov)

        # Unroll the small intra-tile feature loops to increase ILP and
        # enable better register reuse of centered values.
        # (Here p and q refer to the intra-tile indices after blocking.)
        unroll(p, 4)
        unroll(q, 4)

        # ---- Loop ordering ----
        #
        # Hoist the tile loops so the execution order is:
        #   for P, for Q, for K, for p, for q, for k
        # This keeps a cov tile resident in cache while we stream over
        # sample tiles, amortizing data[k,*] loads across many (p,q)
        # accumulations.
        hoist(P)
        hoist(Q)
        hoist(K)

    # =================================
    # Additional semantic notes
    # =================================
    #
    # # No explicit centered-data buffer:
    # #   We compute (data[k,f] - mean[f]) on the fly inside the covariance
    # #   sum instead of materializing a full N×M "centered" array. This
    # #   preserves the mathematics, reduces memory footprint to within the
    # #   original (data + cov + mean) plus a small constant factor, and
    # #   trades a cheap subtraction for a large reduction in memory traffic.
    #
    # # Symmetry:
    # #   Restricting the COV loops to q >= p and then assigning
    # #   cov[q,p] = cov[p,q] exactly matches the original C code behavior,
    # #   which computes only the upper triangle and mirrors it. This
    # #   halves the number of dot products relative to a naïve full-M×M
    # #   computation while preserving correctness.

```text
domain:
    s: dim in [0, N)        # sample index (rows of the input matrix)
    f: dim in [0, M)        # feature index for column means
    p: dim in [0, M)        # row index in covariance matrix
    q: dim in [0, M)        # column index in covariance matrix

data:
    # Input data matrix: C code uses data[N][M] with data[i][j] contiguous in j.
    # We model this as row‑major: samples (s) are rows, features (f) are columns.
    data[s, f]: in DATA_TYPE
        = (s, f) -> s * M + f      # N×M, row-major, f is the fast-varying dimension

    # Column means. In the original C kernel this is a 1D array mean[M].
    mean[f]: temp DATA_TYPE
        = (f) -> f                 # logical layout only; initial contents unused

    # Covariance matrix cov[M][M], stored row‑major.
    cov[p, q]: out DATA_TYPE
        = (p, q) -> p * M + q      # M×M, row-major, q is the fast-varying dimension

parameters:
    float_n: DATA_TYPE                 # equals (DATA_TYPE) N
    inv_float_n: DATA_TYPE             # 1.0 / float_n, precomputed scalar
    inv_float_n_minus_1: DATA_TYPE     # 1.0 / (float_n - (DATA_TYPE)1), precomputed scalar

computation:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    # 1) Compute column means: mean[f] = (1/N) * sum_s data[s,f]
    # ----------------------------------------------------------
    mean_phase:
        for f in [0, M):
            mean[f] = inv_float_n * sum(s in [0, N), data[s, f])

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2) Compute covariance on the upper triangle and mirror to lower
    #
    #    For all p, q:
    #        cov(p,q) = 1/(N-1) * sum_s (data[s,p] - mean[p]) *
    #                                    (data[s,q] - mean[q])
    #
    #    We only *compute* for q >= p, then set cov[q,p] = cov[p,q].
    #    This halves the arithmetic vs computing the full M×M reduction,
    #    but the final cov matrix is still fully populated and symmetric.
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------
    cov_phase:
        for p in [0, M):
            for q in [p, M):
                cov[p, q] = inv_float_n_minus_1 *
                             sum(s in [0, N),
                                 (data[s, p] - mean[p]) *
                                 (data[s, q] - mean[q]))
                cov[q, p] = cov[p, q]

optimization:
    # ==========================================================
    # Mean computation optimizations (mean_phase)
    # ==========================================================
    # The input is row‑major in (s,f), so we want to stream over s
    # (samples/rows) and access f (features/columns) contiguously.
    # Conceptually, we expand the reduction and iterate as:
    #   for s:
    #     for f:
    #       mean[f] += data[s,f]
    # This is expressed via a loop interchange and tiling in f.

    # Tile the feature dimension to improve cache locality and give
    # coarse-grain work units to threads.
    # TM_mean is a tunable tile size (e.g., 64 or 128).
    block(f, Fm, TM_mean)

    # Execute feature tiles at an outer level, then iterate within tiles.
    hoist(Fm)

    # Within each sample-iteration, process features contiguously.
    # This corresponds to interchanging the original (f,s) order into (s,f).
    interchange(f, s)

    # Parallelize the outer feature tiles across CPU cores.
    parallelize(Fm)

    # Vectorize over contiguous features inside each tile.
    # V_mean is chosen to match the SIMD width for DATA_TYPE (e.g., 8 for AVX2 float).
    vectorize(f, V_mean)

    # ==========================================================
    # Covariance computation optimizations (cov_phase)
    # ==========================================================
    # Overall goal:
    #   - Exploit that data[s,*] is contiguous in f to reuse each input
    #     row across many cov[p,q] updates.
    #   - Block the (p,q) space so that a TP×TQ submatrix of cov and
    #     the necessary columns of mean fit in cache.
    #   - Block the reduction over s so that partial sums for a tile
    #     are kept hot in cache/registers.
    #   - Parallelize across independent covariance tiles.
    #   - Vectorize along q (the fast-varying, row-major dimension of cov).

    # Block the covariance output dimensions into tiles of size TP×TQ.
    # TP, TQ are tunable (e.g., 32–64) to fit a TP×TQ block of cov in L2/L3.
    block(p, P, TP)          # P indexes covariance row-tiles
    block(q, Q, TQ)          # Q indexes covariance col-tiles

    # Block the reduction dimension s so that we accumulate over TS
    # samples at a time. TS is chosen so that the working set
    # (TS rows of data restricted to [P,Q] features) and the
    # TP×TQ partial cov tile fit into cache.
    block(s, S, TS)

    # Hoist tile loops outward so the high-level iteration space is:
    #   for each tile P:
    #     for each tile Q (with q >= p):
    #       initialize cov[P,Q] tile
    #       for each sample tile S:
    #         accumulate contributions of data[S,*] into cov[P,Q]
    hoist(P)
    hoist(Q)
    hoist(S)

    # Parallelize across covariance row-tiles. Each P tile (and its
    # corresponding upper-triangular Q tiles) is independent, so we
    # can safely distribute P across threads.
    parallelize(P)

    # Within each (P,Q,S) tile, keep q as the innermost loop to match
    # the row-major layout of cov and enable unit-stride vector loads/stores.
    # This corresponds to an inner-loop order: for p in tile_P, for q in tile_Q.
    interchange(q, s)        # ensure that inside each S tile we iterate q innermost

    # Vectorize the inner q loop when updating cov[p,q].
    # V_cov is chosen according to the SIMD width (e.g., 8 or 16).
    vectorize(q, V_cov)

    # Unroll a small factor of the reduction over samples within each
    # S tile to reduce loop overhead and improve instruction-level
    # parallelism. U_s is a small tunable factor (e.g., 4).
    unroll(s, U_s)

    #  - No parallelization is done across the reduction dimension s,
    #    so reduction associativity issues are avoided.
    #  - We do not allocate a full N×M "centered" array; centered
```

domain:
    # N: number of samples (rows), M: number of features (columns)
    s: dim in [0, N)      # sample index (row of the data matrix)
    f: dim in [0, M)      # feature index used for mean/centering
    i: dim in [0, M)      # covariance row index (feature)
    j: dim in [0, M)      # covariance column index (feature)

data:
    # Store data column-major so that traversing samples (s) for a fixed feature is contiguous.
    # This matches the dominant access pattern in both the mean and covariance reductions.
    #
    # data[s, f] corresponds to C code data[s][f].
    # Layout: all N samples for feature f are contiguous:
    #   offset(s, f) = f * N + s
    data[s, f]: in DATA_TYPE = (s, f) -> f * N + s

    # Column means: size M, trivially laid out.
    mean[f]: temp DATA_TYPE = f -> f

    # Full MxM covariance matrix. Stored row-major (rows in i, columns in j),
    # which is convenient for iterating over j inside a fixed i.
    #   offset(i, j) = i * M + j
    cov[i, j]: out DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * M + j

parameters:
    float_n: DATA_TYPE              # equals N in the calling code
    # Precompute reciprocals once to replace many divides with multiplies.
    inv_float_n: DATA_TYPE          # = 1 / float_n
    inv_float_nm1: DATA_TYPE        # = 1 / (float_n - 1)

computation:
    # 1. Compute column means:
    #
    #   mean[f] = (1 / float_n) * sum_{s=0..N-1} data[s, f]
    #
    # This matches:
    #   mean[j] = 0;
    #   for (i = 0; i < N; i++) mean[j] += data[i][j];
    #   mean[j] /= float_n;
    mean_compute:
        for f:
            mean[f] = inv_float_n * sum(s in [0, N), data[s, f])

    # 2. Compute covariance:
    #
    #   cov[i, j] = (1 / (float_n - 1)) *
    #               sum_{s=0..N-1} (data[s, i] - mean[i]) * (data[s, j] - mean[j])
    #
    # This is mathematically equivalent to the Halide code:
    #   cov_sum(i, j) = sum_k centered(i, k) * centered(j, k);
    #   cov(i, j) = cov_sum(i, j) / (float_n - 1)
    # with centered(s, f) = data[s, f] - mean[f].
    cov_compute:
        for i, j:
            cov[i, j] = inv_float_nm1 *
                        sum(s in [0, N),
                            (data[s, i] - mean[i]) *
                            (data[s, j] - mean[j]))

dependencies:
    # The covariance step depends on the completed mean vector.
    for f in [0, M):
        mean_compute(f) -> cov_compute(i, j)  for all i in [0, M), j in [0, M)

optimization:
    # -----------------------------
    # Scalar precomputations
    # -----------------------------
    # Hoist the reciprocal computations out of all loops; they are pure scalars.
    hoist(inv_float_n)
    hoist(inv_float_nm1)

    # -----------------------------
    # Mean computation optimizations
    # -----------------------------

    # Access pattern here is:

    #     sum over s of data[s, f]
    # With data laid out as (s, f) -> f*N + s, the inner loop over s is contiguous.
    #
    # Tile features (f) to create coarse-grain tasks and expose parallelism.
    # F is the tile index over features, f_inner iterates within a tile.
    # TR (tile over samples) is chosen to fit the working-set for one column into L1/L2.
    #
    # Tunable constants (for a 32-core x64 with large caches):
    #   F_tile = 32   # features per task

    # Vector width 8 is a good default for single-precision on AVX2 (256b) or
    # for doubles on AVX-512 (512b); it is just a suggestion here.
    #
    # mean_compute:
    block(f, F, 32)           # split f into tiles of size 32: F (outer), f (inner)
    hoist(F)                  # make F the outermost loop for this stage
    parallelize(F)            # run feature tiles in parallel across cores

    block(s, S, 256)          # process samples in blocks to improve cache locality
    vectorize(S, 8)           # vectorize across contiguous samples within each block

    # -----------------------------
    # Covariance computation optimizations
    # -----------------------------
    #
    # cov[i, j] = inv_float_nm1 * sum_s (...) is a symmetric MxM Gram matrix.
    # We keep the full computation (no symmetry shortcut) to preserve the original
    # arithmetic pattern, but we reorganize loops for locality and parallelism.
    #
    # We use 3D blocking over (i, j, s):
    #   - I, J: tiles over feature indices (rows/cols of cov)
    #   - S: tiles over samples
    #
    # This improves reuse of mean[i], mean[j], and of data[s, i]/data[s, j] inside

    #
    # Tunable constants:

    #   J_tile = 32
    #   S_tile = 128

    block(i, I, 32)           # tile covariance rows
    block(j, J, 32)           # tile covariance columns
    block(s, S, 128)          # tile samples (reduction dimension)

    # Make the tile loops over I and J outermost to create large independent tasks.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # Parallelize over covariance-row tiles; each (I, J) tile is independent.
    parallelize(I)

    # Keep the reduction over S as the innermost hot loop and vectorize it;
    # this exploits that data[s, i] is contiguous in s due to the column-major layout.
    vectorize(S, 8)

    # Within each tile, unroll small inner loops over j to amortize loop overhead and

    unroll(j, 4)
